items.title: New survey finds enterprises trapped between legacy software and AI modernization
items.summary: Throughout my career in cybersecurity and infrastructure protection — both in government and now at Google Cloud — I have consistently seen that friction between new and existing technology is often a barrier to progress. A new piece of software or service may work wonderfully on its own but then it’s placed within a complex, interconnected IT environment and lost in the operational inertia. Today, enterprise technology is experiencing a historic transformation. Organizations globally are moving beyond integrating AI and LLMs, and are now utilizing AI to power autonomous, agentic workflows. Nearly 90% of the Fortune 100 are already using Gemini Enterprise to build, scale and govern agents. But as AI systems begin to plan, execute multi-step processes, and work alongside human teams, leaders are confronting this same tension between cutting-edge and legacy technology. items.title: Doors Open at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 in SLC
Run cost-effective, always-on agents to monitor your environment: the engineering behind Watchers
items.summary: Alert rules are great for the failures you can predict, but they fall short on the ones you can't. With the advent of modern AI, you might think the solution is to swarm your stack with agents that monitor every last detail, but that can quickly lead to astronomical bills. And those are the gaps Watchers fill: catching what alerts miss while keeping costs in control. Generally Available as of ObservabilityCON 2026 , Watchers are always-on agents in Grafana Assistant . You describe what to monitor (in natural language) and pick your data sources, and the watcher learns what "normal" looks like and tells you when you drift from that state. Ultimately, this helps you surface problems without needing an alert, giving you wider coverage and more confidence in your system. But how do we keep Watchers cost-effective for our customers, especially in comparison to building your own agent that runn around the clock? items.title: Now generally available: GKE dynamic slicing for higher resilience, and efficiency for TPUs
items.summary: Running large-scale AI workloads on TPU and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) requires infrastructure that adapts as fast as your models change. Dynamic Slicing is generally available on GKE, which decouples logical TPU slice formation from physical nodepool provisioning. Compared to creating a static nodepool for each TPU slice, dynamic slicing reduces AI workload startup times by up to 5x and workload recovery by 4.5x — maximizing TPU goodput, efficiency, and workload resilience at scale. Beyond one workload, one nodepool Previously, managing TPU capacity at GKE standard required separate, fixed TPU slice topology nodepools, increasing startup times and complexity while preventing multi-host nodepools from hosting multiple AI workloads. Changing workload needs meant manually deleting and recreating nodepools. Additionally, this tight coupling created large failure domains where a single hardware fault crashed an entire slice, slowing recovery while reprovisioning. items.title: Introducing TPU Sync: Fast KV cache and weight transfer for inference and RL on TPU
items.summary: As frontier AI evolves from stateless single-turn prompts to million-token agents, disaggregated serving, and continuous reinforcement learning (RL), the primary bottleneck in AI infrastructure has shifted from raw compute to orchestrating live model state — both the contextual state held in massive key-value (KV) caches during inference and the parameter state updated and broadcast from trainers to rollout samplers during RL. Whenever this state is trapped inside a single chip's memory or stalled on network transfers, AI accelerators sit idle. We designed TPU Sync from first principles to serve as the model-state layer across TPU clusters — built on the architectural insight that accelerator High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), host DRAM, shared storage, and the data center network (DCN) should operate as a single, co-designed memory hierarchy. An open-source, native C++ library, TPU Sync moves TPU-tiled tensors directly across this hierarchy with asynchronous DMA transfers that overlap data movement with active computation. For inference, it decouples TPU compute from network backpressure

items.summary: Today, we are thrilled to announce the general availability (GA) of Cloud Pathways ( Pathways on Cloud ) on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) as a core runtime pillar of the Google Cloud AI Hypercomputer . Originally engineered by Google DeepMind to train and serve Google's frontier models — including Gemini — Pathways is our distributed machine-learning runtime designed for massive, heterogeneous accelerator fleets. In fact, over the last 90 days alone, leading AI companies and global enterprises have processed more than 130 million Cloud TPU chip-hours using Pathways on GKE, across a broad range of TPU generations. With Cloud Pathways, every Google Cloud customer can use the same single-controller runtime, colocated Python sidecars, and elastic fault tolerance that power Google's largest AI workloads. ## End User Changelog

### 🛑 Breaking changes 🛑

- `all`: Remove the deprecated SignalFx receiver. Use the OTLP receiver instead. (#51934)
- `connector/service_graph`: Remove deprecated feature gates connector.servicegraph.legacyLatencyMetricNames and connector.servicegraph.legacyLatencyUnitMs (#52246)
- `exporter/signalfx`: Stop producing `disk_ops.total` and `disk_ops.pending` metrics with the default translation rules. (#52729)
  Use `system.disk.operations` instead of `disk_ops.total`. It is sent by default as a cumulative counter, so the per-period
  number of operations on a host can be charted with SignalFlow, for example:
  ```
  data('system.disk.operations', rollup='delta').sum(by=['host.name'])
  ```
  Use `system.disk.pending_operations` instead of `disk_ops.pending`. Both are excluded by default, so replace
  `disk_ops.pending` with `system.disk.pending_operations` in `include_metrics`:
  ```yaml
  exporters:
    signalfx:
      include_metrics:
        - metric_name: system.disk.pending_operations
  ```
  
- `pkg/coreinternal`: Promote internal.coreinternal.goldendataset.EmitV1DatabaseConventions and internal.coreinternal.goldendataset.DontEmitV0DatabaseConventions feature gates from Alpha to Beta. (#52690)
  The gates are now enabled by default, so goldendataset generates db.system.name (semconv v1.40.0)
  instead of the deprecated db.system (semconv v1.28.0). The migration remains reversible by disabling
  the gates.
  
- `pkg/coreinternal`: Promote internal.coreinternal.goldendataset.EmitV1NetworkConventions and internal.coreinternal.goldendataset.DontEmitV0NetworkConventions feature gates to Stable. (#52503)
  The gates can no longer be disabled. goldendataset now always generates `network.local.address`,
  `network.peer.address`, and `server.address`, and no longer generates the deprecated `net.host.ip`,
  `net.peer.ip`, `http.host`, and `http.server_name` attributes.
  
- `pkg/coreinternal`: Promote internal.coreinternal.goldendataset.EmitV1RPCConventions and internal.coreinternal.goldendataset.DontEmitV0RPCConventions feature gates to Stable. (#52219)
  The gates can no longer be disabled. goldendataset now always generates `rpc.method` and
  `service.peer.name`, and no longer generates the deprecated `rpc.service` and `peer.service`
  attributes.

### Images and binaries here: https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-releases/releases/tag/v0.165.0

## End User Changelog

### 🛑 Breaking changes 🛑

- `pkg/confighttp`: Remove deprecated fields `IdleConnTimeout`, `MaxIdleConns`, `MaxIdleConnsPerHost`, `DisableKeepAlives`. (#15973)

### 🚀 New components 🚀

- `pkg/xreceiverhelper`: Add xreceiverhelper with an `ObsReport` that reports profile sample metrics per sample type. (#16251)
  `ObsReport.EndProfilesOpBySampleType` records the
  `otelcol_receiver_{accepted,refused,failed}_profile_samples` metrics with an additional
  `sample_type` attribute, formatted as "type:unit", as a single payload can hold multiple profiles
  with different sample types. Use `ProfileSampleCountsByType` to compute the sample counts before
  the profiles are passed to the next consumer, as the data may be mutated downstream.
  The OTLP receiver now uses `EndProfilesOpBySampleType`.
  

### 💡 Enhancements 💡

- `pkg/configmiddleware`: allow to override the dialer used by confighttp.ToClient and configgrpc.ToClient (#16019)
- `pkg/featuregate`: Allow underscores in feature gate IDs. (#16243)
- `pkg/pdata`: Improve performance of pcommon.Map Get, Range, and All functions. (#16282, #16321)
- `pkg/pdata`: Reduce number of allocations when updating an oneof primitive (#16226)
- `pkg/service`: Service now supports configuring additional resource detectors for internal telemetry as per the update to otelconf v0.26.0. (#15869)
- `pkg/service`: Warn at startup when a pipeline combines the batch processor with exporterhelper batching. (#15965)
  Detection does not cross connectors or inspect exporter wrappers that hide exporterhelper's batching capability.
- `pkg/xprocessorhelper`: Instrument `xprocessorhelper.NewProfiles` with `otelcol_processor_incoming_items`, `otelcol_processor_outgoing_items`, and `otelcol_processor_internal_duration`, consistent with the other signal constructors. (#15523)
- `processor/memory_limiter`: Add `garbage_collector` config section to allow disabling forced garbage collection via `enabled` field. (#15081)
- `processor/queue_batch`: Promote the queue_batch processor to beta for traces, metrics, and logs, and to alpha for profiles. (#12022)
- `processor/queue_batch`: Report queue and batch metrics as processor metrics (#14038)

### 🧰 Bug fixes 🧰

- `cmd/mdatagen`: Fix panic in `Attribute.TestValue()` and `Attribute.TestValueTwo()` when handling single-element or empty enum attributes. (#15644)
- `cmd/mdatagen`: Fix generated metrics tests failing when a metric migration's `through_gates` feature gates are promoted past alpha. (#16249)
  The generated tests now explicitly set the migration feature gates for each test case and restore
  their previous state on cleanup, instead of assuming the gates are disabled by default.
  When a gate's stage forbids the state a case needs, such as disabling a stable gate, the metrics-builder
  test skips only its gate-dependent count and warning asse

items.title: Only include resource detectors you need by building your own Collector
items.summary: There are many reasons for building your own OpenTelemetry Collector distribution. The existing distributions are designed to be broadly useful, which means they include many more components than what an individual deployment uses. Building your own gives you the ability to select only the components you care about, add your own custom components, and control exactly what ends up in the binary you run in production. One of the reasons I prefer to build my own distribution is to limit the size of the binary I have to ship around and to ensure that the least amount of dependencies are included. Fewer dependencies means a smaller binary, a smaller attack surface, and fewer third-party modules to track when a vulnerability is disclosed. The OpenTelemetry Collector Builder (ocb) makes this possible: you write a manifest file in YAML to select the components you care about, and ocb compiles them into the resulting binary.

What’s new with Grafana variables: less clutter, easier reuse across dashboards, and more
items.summary: Template variables are one of the most used features in Grafana, providing users with a dropdown to turn one dashboard into hundreds: pick a different cluster , region , or service , and every panel updates. For most of Grafana's history, variables had a single home at the top of the dashboard. Each dashboard had one flat list of variables, and that list was shared by every panel on it. But as dashboards grew in size and number, those controls became harder to organize and maintain. The top of a dashboard could get crowded with dropdowns that only applied to certain panels, while shared controls were copied across dashboards and had to be updated individually. To address these challenges, we’ve rolled out two new features in Grafana: Section-level variables for rows and tabs (generally available): these variables let you place controls near the panels they affect, reducing clutter at the top of the dashboard. items.title: Semantic aggregation over millions of rows in BigQuery with AI.AGG
items.summary: For more than a decade, BigQuery has helped set standards for structured data aggregation, calculating financial sums, counting active users, and computing historical averages at a petabyte scale in seconds. But as modern enterprises become inundated with unstructured data — application logs, customer service transcripts, product imagery, and diagnostic reports — a critical gap has emerged. Historically, relational SQL engines have lacked the native ability to aggregate, synthesize, and extract overarching semantic themes from millions of rows of text and multimodal data. While BigQuery recently introduced powerful row-level AI functions (like AI.GENERATE and AI.CLASSIFY), analyzing massive datasets holistically presents a unique architectural challenge: the large language model (LLM) context window. Even with advanced foundation models like Gemini, you cannot pass millions of rows into a single prompt without triggering severe truncation or hard execution failures. items.title: Powering open infrastructure for autonomous agents
items.summary: As AI shifts from human scale to agent scale , from systems of record to systems of action , and from simple requests to complex agentic workflows , the workload underneath your platform changes completely. An agent works in a continuous, stateful loop: It proposes an action, spins up subagents, executes code or tool calls inside a sandbox, and feeds the results back into the model for the next turn. Running that loop at scale requires the same open foundation and neutral governance that Kubernetes and the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) brought to containers in the 2010s. Today, we are announcing the donation of Agent Substrate , gVisor , and OpenRL , three open source projects that started at Google, to the CNCF following their acceptance last month into the CNCF Sandbox. To bring this open stack into managed production and accelerate it across TPUs and GPUs, we are also announcing that Agent Substrate has reached its 1.0 milestone and is now generally available as Agent Substrate on GKE . items.title: Deckhouse Prom++ v0.8.18
items.summary: Fixes
items.release_notes:
### Fixes
1. **External labels no longer overwrite existing series labels.** Merging external labels for remote write and WAL replay now preserves the series' own non-empty values, so output relabeling sees the original labels and does not unexpectedly drop or rename series (#552).
2. **C++ stream errors no longer terminate the process during cleanup.** Restoring a stream's exception mask could throw while an I/O error was already being handled, causing termination. Stream cleanup now preserves the original error and stream state without throwing a second exception (#565).
3. **Go updated to 1.26.10**, closing GO-2026-6809 (CVE-2026-111943) in `crypto/x509`: certificate verification now rejects known compromised intermediate certificates. Both the CI image and the werf build pin the new version.
4. **Go network dependencies updated.** `golang.org/x/net` is updated to v0.62.0 together with the related `golang.org/x/*` dependencies, including security fixes (#567).
5. **Federation reads the latest samples from the active head again.** Zero-length queries such as `/federate` requests no longer skip the active head merely because its newest sample predates the query time, fixing empty federation responses introduced by the head time-range optimization (#571).

### Performance
1. **Label matching on persisted blocks allocates less memory.** Matching postings offsets are collected compactly before allocating the exact number of iterators, reducing temporary allocations while building query results (#555).

items.title: When the Kubernetes API went silent: A three-layer networking mystery
items.summary: Every support engineer has a case that stays with them. The one that comes up at team lunches. The one where, even after it's resolved, you find yourself staring at a packet capture at midnight just to make sure you really understand what happened. This is that case. It started in January 2026 with a support ticket that read deceptively simply: pods are intermittently failing to reach the Kubernetes API server. The error was a familiar-looking timeout. The customer had already ruled out their own operators. What none of us knew yet was that we were looking at three separate bugs — in three different layers of the stack — all conspiring to produce the same symptom at the same time. By the time it was over, around 800 developers had been blocked from deploying to production for weeks on end, and GKE clusters across europe-west had ground to a halt. In a race to fix the problem, we involved engineers across Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Private Service Connect, networking, hostnet, kernel, and the Linux upstream community, who together tracked down not one but three distinct root caus

items.title: OpenTelemetry eBPF Instrumentation reaches v1.0.0
items.summary: We’re excited to announce v1.0.0 of OpenTelemetry eBPF Instrumentation—OBI! OBI brings OpenTelemetry observability to running Linux applications without requiring changes to their source code. It uses eBPF, together with runtime-specific instrumentation, to capture application metrics and traces across services, languages, and frameworks. You can start with request rates, errors, latency, and service dependencies, then build deeper visibility as your needs grow. This release fulfills the flagship goal we set for 2026 : establishing a stable foundation for OBI. It represents a year of expanding instrumentation coverage, improving correctness, strengthening release tooling, and building the compatibility and telemetry migration practices that users need to operate OBI over time.

items.title: Faster, smaller checkpoints: the File Log receiver now uses protobuf
items.summary: If you run the File Log receiver with a storage extension, the Collector writes a checkpoint every time it polls your log files. That checkpoint is how the receiver remembers where it stopped reading, so a restart does not lose or duplicate logs. For years that checkpoint format was JSON. Starting with OpenTelemetry Collector Contrib v0.164.0, checkpoints are always written as protobuf. On our benchmarks, saving a checkpoint is almost 5 times faster, loading one is more than 5 times faster, and the checkpoint itself is about 35% smaller.

items.summary: What do you need to orchestrate high-density concurrent AI agents? As we transition from static requests toward autonomous agentic workflows, the need for secure, high-density sandboxes is pushing conventional infrastructure far beyond its architectural breaking point. This transition is driving top-tier research labs to demand infrastructure at unprecedented scale — often up to one million concurrent code-execution sandboxes! At this scale, the efficiency of your Kubernetes networking infrastructure directly impacts the economic viability of an agentic initiative. In advanced workflows like reinforcement learning (RL), extreme pod churn can mean thousands of isolated sandboxes spinning up and down every minute. To make sure that valuable GPUs and TPUs are spending their time executing models rather than waiting on sandboxes to initialize, you need sub-second provisioning and extreme compute density. items.title: How to troubleshoot GKE workloads faster with VPC Flow Logs
items.summary: Having visibility into your network traffic is essential to operating Kubernetes environments effectively. When a service slows down or loses connectivity, knowing who is talking to whom lets you narrow the problem down quickly. In a standard cloud network, flow logs provide that view by recording connections between IP addresses, ports, and protocols. In Kubernetes, however, pods are temporary. Their IP addresses change constantly as pods scale, crash, or move between nodes, so a raw log entry showing 10.4.2.18 talking to 10.4.8.44 tells you little about which workload (and pod) owned that address, what namespace it was in, or what application it was trying to reach. By the time you search your cluster, the pod may already be gone! In a Google Cloud environment, VPC Flow Logs closes this gap at the network layer. Google Cloud's virtual network already sees every connection a pod makes, so each sampled flow is recorded with the Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) metadata behind the IP address: pod, workload, namespace, and service. You can enable streaming functionality for ScaNN vector indexes by setting the scann.satisfy limit parameter to relaxed order . items.summary: The OpenTelemetry Transformation Language (OTTL) is now v1. Starting with opentelemetry-collector-contrib v0.164.0, OTTL is stable for traces, metrics, and logs. The release of v1 means OTTL meets the Collector’s ‘stable’ stability criteria for testing, benchmarking, documentation, and telemetry. It also comes with a compatibility promise for all of 1.x. If you write OTTL statements, the syntax and the standard functions stay backward compatible. If you build your own components on top of OTTL, the Go API will also remain compatible.

items.title: Agent Observability FAQ: Understand the value of monitoring, evaluating, and improving your AI agents
items.summary: Agents have quickly become part of the tech landscape as organizations embrace AI across their businesses. But embracing agents also means embracing the monitoring best practices that have long been part of engineers' workflows: tracking performance, catching errors, and responding to incidents But it doesn't stop there. Agents also introduce new challenges. They can give different answers to the same question, be confidently wrong without throwing an error, and turn one request into a long chain of model and tool calls that’s hard to debug. A small prompt change can shift behavior as much as a code deploy. And because agents act on what they read, they open the door to new risks like prompt injection and leaked sensitive data. ### 🛑 Breaking changes 🛑

- `connector/service_graph`: Remove stable connector.servicegraph.virtualNode gate (#52239)
- `exporter/prometheus`: Always preserve leading and consecutive underscores in label names. (#50429)
  Remove `-pkg.translator.prometheus.PermissiveLabelSanitization` from `--feature-gates`; disabling this gate now causes a startup error.
  
- `exporter/prometheus_remote_write`: Always preserve leading and consecutive underscores in label names. (#50429)
  Remove `-pkg.translator.prometheus.PermissiveLabelSanitization` from `--feature-gates`; disabling this gate now causes a startup error.

  `code.function.name` and `code.file.path` are now emitted instead of `code.function` and `code.filepath` by default.
  The gates no longer control the `event.name` resource attribute, which is always emitted.
  
- `pkg/coreinternal`: Promote internal.coreinternal.goldendataset.DontEmitV0HTTPConventions and internal.coreinternal.goldendataset.EmitV1HTTPConventions feature gates to Beta (#45293, #45089)

items.title: The case for OpenTelemetry maintainership
items.summary: I believe OpenTelemetry’s primary constraint isn’t ideas, code contributions, or adoption, but maintainers. About me I’ve been working on OpenTelemetry since early 2021. I’m a maintainer of opentelemetry-java, opentelemetry-configuration, and opentelemetry-injector, and a member of the Technical Committee. In that time I’ve worked at two observability companies, New Relic and now Grafana Labs, in roles with a charter to work on OpenTelemetry while also engaging in internal engineering efforts that depend on it. This post is my opinion, informed by involvement in a lot of different OpenTelemetry projects and by watching various contributors come and go.

items.release_notes:
## [v1.155.0](https://github.com/VictoriaMetrics/VictoriaMetrics/releases/tag/v1.155.0)

Released at 2026-10-23

**Update Note 1:** `vmselect` in [VictoriaMetrics cluster](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/cluster-victoriametrics/): `/admin/tenants` requests without `start` and `end` query args now return tenants for the current day. This is a breaking change because previously it was expected to return all tenants. If you still need to retrieve all tenants, set the `start` and `end` params so that the resulting time range fully includes the `-retentionPeriod`. Also note that [vmctl](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/vmctl/victoriametrics/) is known to send requests to `/admin/tenants` under the hood when migrating data between VictoriaMetrics deployments. Therefore, make sure that you run `vmctl` with both `*-filter-time-start` and `*-filter-time-end` params. See the updated [URL format](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/cluster-victoriametrics/#url-format) and [#11791](https://github.com/VictoriaMetrics/VictoriaMetrics/issues/11791) for details.

* SECURITY: upgrade Go builder from Go1.27.2 to Go1.27.3. See [the list of issues addressed in Go1.27.3](https://github.com/golang/go/issues?q=milestone%3AGo1.27.3%20label%3ACherryPickApproved).
* SECURITY: upgrade base docker image (Alpine) from 3.24.2 to 3.24.3. See [Alpine 3.24.4 release notes](https://alpinelinux.org/posts/Alpine-3.21.9-3.22.7-3.23.7-3.24.3-released.html).

* FEATURE: all VictoriaMetrics components: add `-healthcheck` command-line flag, which checks that the running process accepts connections at `-httpListenAddr` and exits with non-zero code if the check fails. This allows setting up Docker `HEALTHCHECK` in images without `curl` or `wget`. See [these docs](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/url-examples/#health) and [VictoriaLogs#1565](https://github.com/VictoriaMetrics/VictoriaLogs/issues/1565).
* FEATURE: all VictoriaMetrics components: expose `process_cpu_cores_host`, `process_cpu_cores_cgroup_quota`, `process_memory_host_bytes` and `process_memory_cgroup_bytes` metrics. Cgroup metrics are `-1` if no cgroup limit is set or the limit cannot be read. See [#11460](https://github.com/VictoriaMetrics/VictoriaMetrics/issues/11460).
* FEATURE: [vmui](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/single-server-victoriametrics/#vmui): deprecate Server URL editing and show a warning when using a saved custom URL. Existing custom URLs continue to work. See [#11735](https://github.com/VictoriaMetrics/VictoriaMetrics/issues/11735).
* FEATURE: [vmui](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/single-server-victoriametrics/#vmui): update the appearance of error, warning, info, and success messages. See [#11736](https://github.com/VictoriaMetrics/VictoriaMetrics/pull/11736).

items.release_notes:
## 0.162.0

### 🛑 Breaking changes 🛑

- `auto-instrumentation`: Block automatic NodeJS instrumentation upgrades across 0.79.0 because of breaking HTTP, network, and database semantic convention changes. (#2542)
  To upgrade, manually set spec.nodejs.image to an image using instrumentation 0.79.0 or higher. See https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-operator/issues/2542 for migration details.

### 🚀 New components 🚀

- `auto-instrumentation`: Add support for auto-instrumentation in PHP applications. (#932)
  Auto-instrumentation in PHP applications is disabled by default in operator. Users can enable it by setting the
  `--enable-php-instrumentation` or `ENABLE_PHP_AUTO_INSTRUMENTATION` environment variable to `true` in operator
  and setting up the annotations `instrumentation.opentelemetry.io/inject-php` and `instrumentation.opentelemetry.io/otel-php-api-version`.
  For more information, please refer to the documentation.
  
- `auto-instrumentation`: Add initial version of autoinstrumentation for ruby (#3762)
  Ruby auto-instrumentation is disabled by default. Enable it with `--enable-ruby-instrumentation=true`.

### 💡 Enhancements 💡

- `collector`: Inject the cluster TLS profile's supported groups as `curve_preferences` into generated collector configurations. (#6893)
  Receivers and extensions with a `tls` block in `spec.config` now get `curve_preferences` defaulted from the
  cluster's TLS security profile `groups`, following the same defaults-only rule as `min_version` and
  `cipher_suites`: values set by the user are never overridden.
  Groups without a collector `curve_preferences` spelling are logged at operator startup and not injected.
  

### 🧰 Bug fixes 🧰

- `operator, target allocator, opamp, auto-instrumentation`: Remove the distrusted emSign root CAs from the operator, target allocator, OpAMP bridge, and Python auto-instrumentation images. (#5802)
  The operator, target allocator, and OpAMP bridge images require Alpine `ca-certificates` 20261020-r0 or later.
  The Python auto-instrumentation image requires `certifi` 2026.10.19 or later and is published as `0.66b1-3`.
  The updated CA bundle removes the distrusted eMudhra emSign roots, including `emSign ECC Root CA - G3`.
  Images are built with Go 1.27.3, which includes the `crypto/x509` security fixes released on 2026-10-19.
  
- `collector`: Include the requesting user's UID and extra fields in the SubjectAccessReviews used to check RBAC privilege escalation. (#5659)
  Authorizers that rely on these fields, such as AKS with Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization, denied the check
  for users who held the required permissions.
  
- `collector, target allocator`: Use pointer for TargetAllocator Telemetry field so omitempty works correctly with encoding/json (#5695)
  Go's encoding/json does not omit zero-value structs with omitempty. The non-pointer
  TelemetryConfig field caused targetAllocator.telemetry to always be serialized du

items.title: Help us understand how you use OpenTelemetry's ecosystem lists
items.summary: Do you use OpenTelemetry’s registry or ecosystem lists? Comment on the issue and tell us which pages you need and why. We are reviewing the future of these pages. Understanding how people use them will help us focus our efforts within the maintainer time available. Which pages are affected? We have frozen new entries and updates to the following lists while we consider retiring or changing them: Registry : libraries, Collector components, and other tools for using and extending OpenTelemetry. Vendors : organizations offering solutions that consume OpenTelemetry. Distributions : third-party distributions of OpenTelemetry components. Integrations : software with OpenTelemetry support. Adopters : organizations using OpenTelemetry. The issue describes the current direction for each list, including retiring the registry in favor of the OpenTelemetry Ecosystem Explorer . The future of the other lists is still being discussed.

items.summary: Security patch release
items.release_notes:
Security patch release
----------------------

Out-of-band security patch release to fix CVE-2026-111943 ([golang/go#82345](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/82345)): upgrades Go to 1.26.10 so that the compromised eMudhra intermediate CA certificates are no longer trusted, and updates all dependencies to their latest patch versions.

Summary of Changes
------------------

**Minor Changes:**
* alibabacloud: support RRSA (RAM Roles for Service Accounts) credentials in the IPAM allocator, alongside static AccessKeys and ECS instance RAM roles (Backport PR cilium/cilium#49474, Upstream PR cilium/cilium#49093, @4n4nd)

**Bugfixes:**
* Allow wildcard CIDR selectors to match nodes when --policy-cidr-match-mode=nodes is configured (Backport PR cilium/cilium#49474, Upstream PR cilium/cilium#47828, @TheBeeZee)
* bpf: nat: fix outer ICMP checksum for ICMP/SCTP NAT error packets (Backport PR cilium/cilium#49474, Upstream PR cilium/cilium#48819, @fds7280)
* CiliumEnvoyConfig now only redirects Services in its own namespace, as documented; service references in CiliumClusterwideEnvoyConfig without a namespace default to "default" again. (Backport PR cilium/cilium#49474, Upstream PR cilium/cilium#49076, @maxskokov)
* datapath: Fix NAT46x64 gateway prefix conversion panic (Backport PR cilium/cilium#49474, Upstream PR cilium/cilium#49177, @HadrienPatte)
* Fix an issue where terminating backends were evicted from BPF maps when trafficDistribution was enabled. (Backport PR cilium/cilium#49474, Upstream PR cilium/cilium#48349, @taesung320)
* Fix invalid L4 checksum on IPv6 ClusterIP reverse NAT for CHECKSUM_PARTIAL packets on kernels < 6.12, affecting the case when packets are bridged/tunneled from the client pod to a remote host (Backport PR cilium/cilium#49474, Upstream PR cilium/cilium#49204, @liuyuan10)
* Fix regression in Cilium 1.20.3 where the Gateway API implementation would incorrectly handle BackendTLSPolicy configurations, leading to high Cilium CPU usage and inability to forward traffic. (Backport PR cilium/cilium#49568, Upstream PR cilium/cilium#49525, @youngnick)
* Fixes an issue in LBIPAM where on service upsert, if IP allocations are not changed the sharing index is not updated. (Backport PR cilium/cilium#49474, Upstream PR cilium/cilium#48938, @0xch4z)
* nodediscovery: in IPAM ENI and Azure modes the operator now treats nodes as running in multi-pool mode from the very first event. (Backport PR cilium/cilium#49390, Upstream PR cilium/cilium#49242, @41ks)
* Reduce transient DNS SERVFAIL/REFUSED for pods that query immediately at startup by pushing/applying Standalone DNS Proxy policy snapshots more frequently (Backport PR cilium/cilium#49474, Upstream PR cilium/cilium#49112, @QxBytes)
* Remove the unused pebble binary from the cilium image to clear its Go standard library vulnerability findings. (Backport PR cilium/cilium#49474, Upstream PR cilium/cilium#49380, @aanm)

**CI Changes:**
* [v1.20] ci: ignore transient xDS mode

## Traces

- Add `Sampler.Shutdown` operation.
  ([#5335](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-specification/pull/5335))
- Clarify that calls to the Development `SpanProcessor.OnEnding` method are not
  allowed after `Shutdown`.
  ([#5316](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-specification/pull/5316))

## Metrics

- Specify that `Shutdown` of the periodic exporting MetricReader MUST include
  the effects of `ForceFlush`.
  ([#5305](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-specification/pull/5305))

## Logs

- Add systemd-journald example mapping to the logs data model appendix and align syslog mapping.
  ([#4995](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-specification/pull/4995))

## Resource

- Update resource detectors to generate entities and indicate resource detectors should be entity-aware
  unless new `OTEL_EXPERIMENTAL_ENTITIES_ENABLED != true`.
  ([#5147](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-specification/pull/5147))

## Entities

- Add in-development entity-resource startup specification.
  ([#5057](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-specification/pull/5057))
- Remove `OTEL_ENTITIES` from general env var configuration spec.
  ([#5147](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-specification/pull/5147))

## Common

- Stabilize Attribute and Attribute Collection representation for non-OTLP.
  ([#5149](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-specification/pull/5149))

## OpenTelemetry Protocol

- Clarify that the OTLP exporter timeout bounds the entire batch export,
  including all request attempts and waits between retries, and that earlier
  caller deadlines take precedence.
  ([#5347](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-specification/pull/5347))

## Compatibility

- Stabilize Prometheus Unknown-typed metric transformation.
  ([#5213](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-specification/pull/5213))
- Stabilize Prometheus Info metric transformation.
  ([#5211](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-specification/pull/5211))

  resource detectors. Other SDK plugin components continue to produce errors
  when missing.

items.title: Strengthening OpenTelemetry security while preserving API stability
items.summary: OpenTelemetry has updated its client versioning policy to make room for security fixes that need to change behavior. Stable SDKs and Contrib components, such as instrumentation libraries and exporters, can now make narrowly scoped, necessary security changes in minor or patch releases, even when those changes affect existing users. Public API compatibility remains protected. The intent is to help users receive security improvements within the major version they already use. Some upgrades may require configuration or operational changes. In such cases, release notes must explain the impact and what to do.

items.title: Deckhouse Prom++ v0.8.17
items.summary: Features
items.release_notes:
### Features
1. **Head query latency can now be broken down by stage.** Instant and range `Select`, `ChunkQuerier` and label names / values queries report per-stage duration and execution counters (`prompp_querier_query_stage_*`) — semaphore wait, LSS lookup, `DataStorage` query, remaining data-load wait and result construction — together with the maximum synchronous call duration across shards (`prompp_querier_query_shard_stage_*`). The labels are fixed (`source`, `operation`, `stage`), bounding cardinality at 188 series. The stage metrics are off by default and enabled with `PROMPP_FEATURES=enable_query_stage_metrics`; the existing `prompp_querier_query_*_duration` histograms keep their names, labels and buckets, now include resource cleanup and semaphore release, and record fractional microseconds (#543).
2. **`label_replace` results are memoized.** Rules and dashboards repeat the same `label_replace` over the same series, and every evaluation used to recompile the regexp and rebuild every labelset. The engine now keeps two bounded LRU caches — result labelsets (keyed by the arguments, the source value and the hash of the source labelset) and compiled regexps — shared by all evaluators, including subqueries. Capacities are set with `PROMPP_FEATURES=label_replace_cache_size=N,label_replace_regex_cache_size=M` (`0` or absent keeps the defaults of 65536 and 128, a negative value turns a cache off); hits, misses, evictions and entries are reported as `prometheus_engine_label_replace_cache_*` (#537).

### Fixes
1. **A failed C++ allocation throws `std::bad_alloc` again.** The jemalloc patch from the GCC 16 migration constructed a `std::bad_alloc` temporary instead of throwing it, so a throwing `operator new` returned `nullptr` on OOM and the failure surfaced later as a null dereference far from the cause (#539).
2. **Setting the pending shrink boundary during rotation no longer holds a P.** The call removes hidden series and rebuilds indexes, taking hundreds of milliseconds; it went through fastcgo, which keeps the P for the whole call and delays Go scheduling and GC stop-the-world coordination. It is now a regular cgo call (#547).
3. **A truncated TSDB chunk now ends with EOF instead of a mis-decoded sample.** The bitstream reader reported a refill as successful even when fewer bits than requested were left, so the last float of a truncated chunk could be returned as a valid sample (#549).

### Performance
1. **The active head is skipped for queries outside its time range.** Head time bounds are now maintained incrementally on append, so the active head's interval is accurate without rescanning the data storage, and the range check applies to it too; it also gained its missing half — a head whose data starts after the query range is no longer queried. When the bounds do need to be computed (WAL load, rotation), they come from the shared timestamp sequences instead of a pass over every series: about 1.2 ms → 7 µs on a 200k-series head (#541, #544)

items.title: Deckhouse Prom++ v0.8.17
items.summary: 1. **Head query latency can now be broken down by stage.** Instant and range `Select`, `ChunkQuerier` and label names / values queries report per-stage duration and execution counters (`prompp_querier_query_stage_*`) — semaphore wait, LSS lookup, `DataStorage` query, remaining data-load wait and result construction — together with the maximum synchronous call duration across shards (`prompp_querier_query_shard_stage_*`). The labels are fixed (`source`, `operation`, `stage`), bounding cardinality at 188 series. The stage metrics are off by default and enabled with `PROMPP_FEATURES=enable_query_stage_metrics`; the existing `prompp_querier_query_*_duration` histograms keep their names, labels and buckets, now include resource cleanup and semaphore release, and record fractional microseconds (#543).
items.release_notes:
### Features
1. **Head query latency can now be broken down by stage.** Instant and range `Select`, `ChunkQuerier` and label names / values queries report per-stage duration and execution counters (`prompp_querier_query_stage_*`) — semaphore wait, LSS lookup, `DataStorage` query, remaining data-load wait and result construction — together with the maximum synchronous call duration across shards (`prompp_querier_query_shard_stage_*`). The labels are fixed (`source`, `operation`, `stage`), bounding cardinality at 188 series. The stage metrics are off by default and enabled with `PROMPP_FEATURES=enable_query_stage_metrics`; the existing `prompp_querier_query_*_duration` histograms keep their names, labels and buckets, now include resource cleanup and semaphore release, and record fractional microseconds (#543).
2. **`label_replace` results are memoized.** Rules and dashboards repeat the same `label_replace` over the same series, and every evaluation used to recompile the regexp and rebuild every labelset. The engine now keeps two bounded LRU caches — result labelsets (keyed by the arguments, the source value and the hash of the source labelset) and compiled regexps — shared by all evaluators, including subqueries. Capacities are set with `PROMPP_FEATURES=label_replace_cache_size=N,label_replace_regex_cache_size=M` (`0` or absent keeps the defaults of 65536 and 128, a negative value turns a cache off); hits, misses, evictions and entries are reported as `prometheus_engine_label_replace_cache_*` (#537).

### Fixes
1. **A failed C++ allocation throws `std::bad_alloc` again.** The jemalloc patch from the GCC 16 migration constructed a `std::bad_alloc` temporary instead of throwing it, so a throwing `operator new` returned `nullptr` on OOM and the failure surfaced later as a null dereference far from the cause (#539).
2. **Setting the pending shrink boundary during rotation no longer holds a P.** The call removes hidden series and rebuilds indexes, taking hundreds of milliseconds; it went through fastcgo, which keeps the P for the whole call and delays Go scheduling and GC stop-the-world coordination. It is now a regular cgo call (#547).
3. **A truncated TSDB chunk now ends with EOF instead of a mis-decoded sample.** The bitstream reader reported a refill as successful even when fewer bits than requested were left, so the last float of a truncated chunk could be returned as a valid sample (#549).

### Performance
1. **The active head is skipped for queries outside its time range.** Head time bounds are now maintained incrementally on append, so the active head's interval is accurate without rescanning the data storage, and the range check applies to it too; it also gained its missing half — a head whose data starts after the query range is no longer queried. When the bounds do need to be computed (WAL load, rotation), they come from the shared timestamp sequences instead of a pass over every series: about 1.2 ms → 7 µs on a 200k-series head (#541, #544).
2. **PromQL vector matching is cheaper in range queries.** Seven upstream engine optimizations were backported: numeric matching signatures instead of string keys, buffers and result sets reused across steps, `labels.Builder` reset only on cache misses, and fewer step-invariant and parenthesis wrappers. On 1,000 series × 120 steps one-to-one joins are 26% faster, `group_left` 28% and `or` 36%, with 10–89% fewer bytes allocated (#545).
3. **Persisted-block reads spend less CPU on XOR decoding and postings.** Upstream fast paths decode regular timestamps, unchanged values and reused XOR windows directly from the bit buffer, and postings intersections skip redundant `Seek` calls: intersections are 30–36% faster and `sum by(job)` over constant and counter data 8–20% faster, while gauge aggregation is about 2–3% slower (#546).
4. **Inverse label matchers on persisted blocks traverse postings directly.** `label!=""`, `label=""` and similar selectors no longer enumerate label values and look up their postings one by one: postings construction is about 27% faster and a selective `Select` up to 25% faster, at the cost of more allocated bytes for broad negative regexps (#550).

### Other
1. **The preallocated v3 catalog log layout is in place, without changing the production format.** The new file has two journal regions and two CRC-protected header slots, restores the append position after a crash and rejects corrupted headers without overwriting the file. Production keeps writing v2; switching journals on compaction and writing v3 will follow (#540).

## Version 2.19.7 Release Notes

Compatible with OpenSearch and OpenSearch Dashboards version 2.19.7

### Enhancements

* Add upper bound for the hot_threads `snapshots` parameter with configurable `monitor.jvm.hot_threads.max_snapshots` cluster setting ([#23144](https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch/pull/23144))
* Add `search.query.max_query_nesting_depth` setting to limit query_string parenthesis nesting depth and prevent StackOverflowError ([#22854](https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch/pull/22854))
* Cap `max_determinized_states` in completion suggester regex and fuzzy options to prevent heap exhaustion ([#22925](https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch/pull/22925))
* Disable Mustache partial template resolution in search templates ([#22440](https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch/pull/22440))
* Reject out-of-range WLM node threshold updates at validation time ([#22678](https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch/pull/22678))

### Bug Fixes

* Fix unbounded recursion in JSON and binary deserialization that could cause StackOverflowError ([#22427](https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch/pull/22427))
* Strengthen scroll_id validation to prevent OOM from crafted scroll IDs with oversized counts ([#22401](https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch/pull/22401))
* Validate `base_path` in fs repository to prevent path traversal outside configured `path.repo` directories ([#22381](https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch/pull/22381))
* Fix handling of unsupported zstd HTTP content encoding in netty4 and nio transports ([#23324](https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch/pull/23324))

### Maintenance

* Bump Jackson to 2.18.9 and Log4j to 2.25.5 ([#22990](https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch/pull/22990))
* Bump Bouncy Castle bc-fips to 2.1.3 ([#23284](https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch/pull/23284))
* Update Netty to 4.1.139.Final ([#22692](https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch/pull/22692), [#23003](https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch/pull/23003), [#23251](https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch/pull/23251))

## [1.21.0](https://github.com/grafana/alloy/compare/v1.20.0...v1.21.0) (2026-10-16)


### ⚠ BREAKING CHANGES

* **otelcol.receiver.kafka:** `otelcol.receiver.kafka` and `otelcol.exporter.kafka` `metadata > retry > max_retries` now defaults to `20` (was `3`) and is now actually applied. Upstream's Kafka client silently ignored it since the franz-go migration. `otelcol.exporter.kafka` now also applies `backoff`. ([#7366](https://github.com/grafana/alloy/issues/7366))
* **otelcol.connector.signaltometrics:** `otelcol.connector.signaltometrics` `error_mode` now defaults to `ignore` (was `propagate`). A failing OTTL expression now skips the record and logs the error instead of dropping the whole payload. Set `error_mode = "propagate"` to restore the previous behavior. ([#7366](https://github.com/grafana/alloy/issues/7366))
* **loki.write:** `loki.write` configurations that set `wal { enabled = true }` now fail to load unless Alloy runs with `--stability.level=experimental`. To keep using the WAL, add `--stability.level=experimental` to the `alloy run` command. To keep the default stability level, remove the `wal` block or set `enabled = false`. ([#7257](https://github.com/grafana/alloy/issues/7257))

## Bug fixes

- `live-store`: Fix a panic in live-store `FindTraceByID` when more spans for the trace arrive while it is being combined with block data and marshalled. ([#8111](https://github.com/grafana/tempo/issues/8111)) (@KR-Ravindra)
  The live trace's `Batches` slice was handed to the trace combiner with spare capacity, so the
  combiner's append and the push path's append wrote different batches into the same slot of the
  live trace's backing array. `Size()` and `Marshal()` then saw different objects and marshalling
  panicked with `slice bounds out of range`.
  
- `query-frontend`: Fix rare cache collision between instant and range metrics queries. ([#7290](https://github.com/grafana/tempo/issues/7290)) (@ruslan-mikhailov)

items.title: Day 0 support for Reflection’s Beam on Google Cloud: 5x faster perf with llm-d and NVIDIA Dynamo

Released under a permissive Apache 2.0 license with BF16 , FP8 , and NVFP4 checkpoints available at launch, Beam sets a new standard for inference efficiency in the 500B-parameter class by solving complex reasoning and coding problems with 3x to 4x higher reasoning compute efficiency than comparable open models. Alongside today’s release, Google Cloud is announcing day 0 support and ready-to-run deployment recipes for serving Beam on Google Cloud AI Hypercomputer and NVIDIA AI Infrastructure. To help developers get the full benefit of Beam’s token efficiency in production, we worked with Reflection to optimize performance of the underlying serving stack using llm-d (with vLLM) and NVIDIA Dynamo (with SGLang) on Google Cloud: "By deploying our Beam model on Google Cloud, we achieved up to 5x higher performance and 8x lower latency to optimize serving of agentic workloads." -

The OpenTelemetry Collector Contrib contains everything in the [opentelemetry-collector release](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/releases/tag/v0.163.0), be sure to check the release notes there as well.

## End User Changelog

### 🛑 Breaking changes 🛑

- `cmd/opampsupervisor`: The supervisor now fails to start when the deprecated `reports_remote_config` capability option is set to `true`. (#49763)
  Remove `reports_remote_config` from the supervisor config; `accepts_remote_config` enables both the AcceptsRemoteConfig and ReportsRemoteConfig OpAMP capabilities. The option will be removed in v0.165.0.
  
- `connector/failover`: Reject empty `condition.error.contains` values and fail over only for matching downstream errors (#44518)
  `condition.error.contains` now requires a list of non-empty strings.
- `exporter/signalfx`: Exclude generated `container_cpu_utilization` metric by default (#51906)
  This metric has been deprecated in favor of `container.cpu.usage`. If `container_cpu_utilization`
  is still required, please add it to the exporter's `include_metrics` configuration option as shown below.
  ```
  signalfx:
    include_metrics:
      - metric_name: container_cpu_utilization
  ```
  
- `extension/google_cloud_logentry_encoding`: Fix Cloud DNS query logs failing to decode when `vmInstanceId` is in exponent notation. `host.id` is now a string taken from `vmInstanceIdString` instead of an int taken from `vmInstanceId`. (#51552)
- `processor/redaction`: Keep every redaction summary attribute intact when data re-enters the processor (#50770)
  Only five of the fourteen summary attributes the processor writes survived a second redaction processor. When data
  passed through one, `redaction.allowed.keys`, `redaction.allowed.count` and the seven `redaction.body.*` attributes
  were treated as unknown keys, deleted, and reported in `redaction.redacted.keys`.
  
  The processor now treats all fourteen as its own bookkeeping rather than as user data, so they are no longer deleted,
  masked, obfuscated or counted as redacted, and the summary accumulates across chained processors as intended.
  Previously a `blocked_key_patterns` or `blocked_values` rule matching one of these attributes replaced the summary
  with a masked value, and with `redact_all_types` enabled it rewrote the `*.count` integers as strings, which made the
  running totals read back as zero at the next hop.
  
  Chaining two processors also reported the same attribute more than once: the allowed and ignored summaries
  describe the record as it currently stands, which every processor re-derives in full, so merging them with an
  upstream value counted one attribute twice. `redaction.allowed.keys` read `email,email` with
  `redaction.allowed.count` of 2 for a single allowed attribute. Those two outcomes now replace the upstream
  value, while the redacted and masked outcomes keep accumulating, because a removed key and an already masked
  value cannot be dete

## End User Changelog

### 💡 Enhancements 💡

- `cmd/builder`: Add `dist.resource.detection.detectors` to the builder config, letting distributions opt into a smaller set of resourcedetectionprocessor detectors via generated go build tags. (#16075)
- `cmd/mdatagen`: Generate exporter queue/batch sender defaults from an opt-in `sending_queue` field in metadata.yaml. See the [batching migration RFC](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/blob/main/docs/rfcs/batching-migration.md). (#15963)
  Declaring `sending_queue` is opt-in; an exporter that omits it is unaffected until it explicitly opts in one at a time during Phase 2 of the migration. Set MDATAGEN_SENDING_QUEUE_OPT_OUT=true to generate the standard default for every undeclared exporter while auditing a whole repository.
- `pkg/pprofile`: Implement Profiles development-version metadata in the OTLP receiver and exporters. (#16147, #16009)
  The receiver rejects malformed, repeated, or unsupported versions before decoding.
  OTLP exporters send the version associated with their compiled-in Profiles schema.
  The version is not configurable, and existing clients without metadata identify
  the initial development version.

## 0.161.0

### 🛑 Breaking changes 🛑

- `opamp`: Use the Kubernetes cluster ID to compute standalone OpAMP Bridge agent instance IDs. (#5689)
  - Existing standalone agents will report new instance IDs after upgrade.
  - The bridge now requires the "get" permission on the "kube-system" namespace to read the cluster ID.
  
- `collector`: Remove the deprecated `--create-rbac-permissions` CLI flag. RBAC permission creation is now exclusively autodetected at startup. (#2588)
  The flag was deprecated in v0.88.0. The operator now always autodetects whether its service account can create ClusterRoles and ClusterRoleBindings.

### 💡 Enhancements 💡

- `collector`: Add `revisionHistoryLimit` field to OpenTelemetryCommonFields to control the number of old ReplicaSets retained for Deployment and StatefulSet workloads, and for the TargetAllocator Deployment. (#0)
- `collector`: Skip the automatic `GOMEMLIMIT` and `GOMAXPROCS` environment variables when the collector config enables the `cgroup_runtime` extension. (#5651)
  The extension sets both variables from the cgroup limits and does nothing when they are already present.
  The deprecated `cgroupruntime` type name is recognized as well.
  Each variable is skipped only while its `gomemlimit.enabled` or `gomaxprocs.enabled` setting is true.
  
- `collector, target allocator`: Add `imagePullSecrets` to the OpenTelemetryCollector and TargetAllocator CRs, passed through to the pod spec of the generated workloads. A target allocator embedded in an OpenTelemetryCollector uses the collector's `imagePullSecrets`. (#4376)
- `collector`: Register the `webhook_event` receiver (alias `webhookevent`) so the operator derives its Service port from `endpoint`, which the receiver requires, and rejects a configuration that omits it. (#5631)

- `collector`: Fix the collector defaulting webhook panicking when `receivers` or `exporters` is missing. (#5735)

items.title: Deckhouse Prom++ v0.8.16
items.summary: Features
items.release_notes:
### Features
1. **Append and WAL latency can now be broken down by stage.** New low-overhead counters report the duration and execution count of caller-side append stages (`prompp_head_append_stage_*`), the maximum duration across shards (`prompp_head_append_shard_stage_*`), and WAL operations (`prompp_shard_wal_stage_*`). The metrics distinguish semaphore waits, relabeling and cache hits or misses, data-storage writes, WAL writes, commits, flushes and syncs without adding a `shard_id` label (#529).
2. **Previously unattributed relabeling and label-storage memory is now visible.** `prompp_scrape_relabeling_caches_bytes` reports scrape and report-state mapping caches per scrape job, with memoized C++ measurements to avoid a cgo call on every steady-state scrape. `prompp_head_cgo_memory_bytes` now reports the ingestion-only input LSS under `allocator="input_lss"`; `allocator="main_lss"` contains only the target LSS, so their sum preserves the previous total (#533).

### Fixes
1. **Persisting a head can no longer read a stale chunk iterator after loading the next batch.** The recoder used to position the next batch before `Loader::load_finalize` could replace a finalized chunk, leaving cached pointers to freed memory. Depending on allocator reuse this caused a crash in `ChunkRecoderIterator`, wrote overlapping chunks that later failed compaction, or skipped a batch that appeared empty before loading. The iterator is now positioned only after the batch has been loaded (#531).
2. **Compaction safely treats empty input and an all-corrupted input set as a no-op.** Both the upstream TSDB compactor path and the Prom++ lcompactor path now return no block instead of dereferencing an empty meta list, panicking, or attempting to write a bogus block. Corrupted blocks remain marked and are excluded from the next plan, so the compaction loop terminates normally (#532, #534).
3. **Two C++ undefined-behaviour paths were hardened.** The WAL timestamp encoding heuristic now uses guarded unsigned arithmetic instead of underflowing, and jemalloc's slab-bitmap exhaustion path aborts on the violated allocator invariant instead of retrying an allocation through an out-of-bounds bitmap access (#535).

## [v1.154.0](https://github.com/VictoriaMetrics/VictoriaMetrics/releases/tag/v1.154.0)

Released at 2026-10-12

**Update Note 1:** [vmauth](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/vmauth/): setups with two chained `vmauth` instances, where the first one authenticates requests via `users` and the second one proxies them via `unauthorized_user` (for example, `VMDistributed` or `VMCluster` managed by [VictoriaMetrics operator](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/operator/)), get an extra 2-3 seconds delay for every request. This is because the second `vmauth` receives the `Authorization` header forwarded by the first one and treats it as an invalid auth token. Upgrade to the [v1.154.1](https://github.com/VictoriaMetrics/VictoriaMetrics/blob/master/docs/victoriametrics/changelog/CHANGELOG.md#v11541) release, where requests aren't delayed if no `users` are configured, or remove the `Authorization` header at the first `vmauth` with `headers: ["Authorization:"]`. See [#11774](https://github.com/VictoriaMetrics/VictoriaMetrics/issues/11774).

**Update Note 2:** `vmstorage` in [VictoriaMetrics cluster](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/cluster-victoriametrics/): `/admin/tenants` requests without `start` and `end` query args (or with zero values) can cause excessive memory usage and OOM crashes of `vmstorage`. Such requests are issued automatically by [vmui](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/single-server-victoriametrics/#vmui) when it is opened via `vmselect`. This is because `vmstorage` [no longer switches to the global index](https://github.com/VictoriaMetrics/VictoriaMetrics/commit/742778ebf1) for queries with long time ranges, so it scans per-day indexes for every day in the whole retention concurrently. Upgrade to [v1.155.0](https://github.com/VictoriaMetrics/VictoriaMetrics/releases/tag/v1.155.0), or roll back to [v1.153.0](https://github.com/VictoriaMetrics/VictoriaMetrics/releases/tag/v1.153.0). See [#11791](https://github.com/VictoriaMetrics/VictoriaMetrics/issues/11791).

**Update Note 3:** [vmsingle](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/single-server-victoriametrics/) and `vmstorage` in [VictoriaMetrics cluster](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/cluster-victoriametrics/): queries and requests to `/api/v1/series`, `/api/v1/labels` and `/api/v1/label/.../values` with long time ranges can cause excessive memory usage and OOM crashes. This is because VictoriaMetrics [no longer switches to the global index](https://github.com/VictoriaMetrics/VictoriaMetrics/commit/742778ebf1) for searches with long time ranges, so it scans per-day indexes for every day in the requested time range concurrently. items.title: Prometheus and OpenTelemetry interoperability in 2026: Survey results
items.summary: We ran a survey asking users of OpenTelemetry and Prometheus how they collect, process, and store metrics. The goal was to understand, with real usage data rather than assumptions, how far the ecosystem has moved and whether the interoperability still causes friction. Key takeaways Interoperability has measurably improved since our 2024 survey : the average ease-of-use rating rose from 3.1 to 3.6, the equivalent of one in two respondents rating a whole category higher, and the share of respondents finding the two hard to use together fell from 29% to 10%. In infrastructure instrumentation, Prometheus exporters remain the most-used method (72%) with OTel receivers close behind (57%), and nearly half of respondents run both at once rather than migrating from one to the other. items.release_notes:
### Features
1. **Append and WAL latency can now be broken down by stage.** New low-overhead counters report the duration and execution count of caller-side append stages (`prompp_head_append_stage_*`), the maximum duration across shards (`prompp_head_append_shard_stage_*`), and WAL operations (`prompp_shard_wal_stage_*`). The metrics distinguish semaphore waits, relabeling and cache hits or misses, data-storage writes, WAL writes, commits, flushes and syncs without adding a `shard_id` label (#529).
2. **Previously unattributed relabeling and label-storage memory is now visible.** `prompp_scrape_relabeling_caches_bytes` reports scrape and report-state mapping caches per scrape job, with memoized C++ measurements to avoid a cgo call on every steady-state scrape. `prompp_head_cgo_memory_bytes` now reports the ingestion-only input LSS under `allocator="input_lss"`; `allocator="main_lss"` contains only the target LSS, so their sum preserves the previous total (#533).

### Fixes
1. **Persisting a head can no longer read a stale chunk iterator after loading the next batch.** The recoder used to position the next batch before `Loader::load_finalize` could replace a finalized chunk, leaving cached pointers to freed memory. Depending on allocator reuse this caused a crash in `ChunkRecoderIterator`, wrote overlapping chunks that later failed compaction, or skipped a batch that appeared empty before loading. The iterator is now positioned only after the batch has been loaded (#531).
2. **Compaction safely treats empty input and an all-corrupted input set as a no-op.** Both the upstream TSDB compactor path and the Prom++ lcompactor path now return no block instead of dereferencing an empty meta list, panicking, or attempting to write a bogus block. Corrupted blocks remain marked and are excluded from the next plan, so the compaction loop terminates normally (#532, #534).
3. **Two C++ undefined-behaviour paths were hardened.** The WAL timestamp encoding heuristic now uses guarded unsigned arithmetic instead of underflowing, and jemalloc's slab-bitmap exhaustion path aborts on the violated allocator invariant instead of retrying an allocation through an out-of-bounds bitmap access (#535).
4. **Go updated to 1.26.9**, closing the twelve standard-library advisories `govulncheck` reports as reachable against the 1.26.8 toolchain the previous release was built with: in `net/http`, HTTP/2 server memory exhaustion through declared `Trailer` fields (GO-2026-6603), HTTP/1 client connection desynchronization after a rejected `CONNECT` (GO-2026-6605), an unbounded `Range` header parse (GO-2026-6609), the HTTP/2 transport accepting malformed framing headers (GO-2026-6610), CPU exhaustion from repeated initial window changes (GO-2026-6611), a double connection-level flow-control refund on reset streams (GO-2026-6612), HTTP/1 server desynchronization after a 2xx `CONNECT` response (GO-2026-6613) and an HPACK encoder race crashing the HTTP/2 server (GO-2026-6617); a memory-limit bypass parsing MIME headers in `net/textproto` and `mime/multipart` (GO-2026-6608); malformed ECH outer extension references in `crypto/tls` (GO-2026-6607); and two JavaScript context-tracking errors in `html/template`, both reachable through the template expander and the web handlers (GO-2026-6599, GO-2026-6600). The thirteenth advisory of this release, `os.Root.Mkdir` following junctions out of the root (GO-2026-6604), is Windows-only and does not apply to the shipped builds. Both the CI image and the werf build pin the new version.
5. **`golang.org/x/net` updated to v0.60.0**, together with the compatible `x/crypto` v0.57.0, `x/mod` v0.41.0, `x/sync` v0.23.0, `x/sys` v0.48.0, `x/term` v0.46.0 and `x/text` v0.42.0. Five of the HTTP/2 defects above also live in `x/net/http2` (GO-2026-6603, GO-2026-6610, GO-2026-6611, GO-2026-6612, GO-2026-6617), and that package is linked into the binaries through `prometheus/common/config`, which configures the HTTP/2 transport of every scrape and remote-write client (#536).
6. **`source-map-js` updated to 1.2.2 in the web UI**, closing GHSA-68fv-2mgg-jv7q — indexed source-map section offsets are read without validation, so a crafted map can stall the event loop. It reaches the shipped UI through `sanitize-html` → `postcss`. The `braces` advisory GHSA-vfj7-8cjw-p6xm has no fixed release and is reachable only through the `sass` compiler and the dev-server proxy, neither of which ends up in the embedded bundle, so it is left in place.

### Performance
1. **WAL v2 commits only the shard whose segment reached its size limit.** Cold shards are no longer forced to emit small segments and perform `write`/`fsync` work whenever a busy shard fills up. WAL v1 retains the commit-all behaviour. The v2 loader now accepts uneven shard segment counts and validates the global segment-ID sequence, including a missing ID 0 and empty shards. items.title: Zero-code trace-log correlation with OBI
items.summary: You get paged. A trace shows a request failing in one of your services, and you know the answer is in the logs — but which log lines belong to that request? If the service never adopted structured logging with trace context, the honest answer is: you grep by timestamp and hope. Your applications don’t change: no SDK, no logging-library configuration, no application rebuild or redeploy.

items.title: October 06, 2026
items.summary: Issue Starting with GKE version 1.36, the default engine for kube-dns is CoreDNS . For Pod IP DNS queries in the . .pod.cluster.local format, CoreDNS returns NXDOMAIN if the specified does not exist. The legacy kubernetes/dns implementation skipped checking the existence of the namespace provided in the segment in these queries. Queries in the . .pod.cluster.local format are not part of the Kubernetes DNS specification . We can't guarantee that uses outside of those specified in the DNS spec will remain consistent across releases. Mitigation: Recommended : Migrate to supported headless Service DNS records ( . . .svc.cluster.local ). Workaround : Ensure the specified in the DNS query exists in the cluster.

### Features
1. **Head IDs are now generated as UUIDv7.** `catalog.DefaultIDGenerator` returns a UUIDv7 instead of a random UUIDv4, falling back to v4 if generation fails. 2. **Prom++ can now report that it is running with a feature set other than the expected one.** The new optional `PROMPP_FEATURES_DEFAULT` environment variable holds the expected set; at startup it is compared with `PROMPP_FEATURES` and the result is exposed as the `prompp_features_differ_from_default` gauge — `1` when they differ, `0` when they match — registered only when the variable is set. A mismatch is also logged at warn level with `added` / `removed` / `changed` fields, so it is clear what exactly drifted. The comparison ignores order, whitespace and empty tokens and compares values by meaning: `default_sample_age_limit=60m` equals `=1h`, `head_read_concurrency` equals `head_read_concurrency=1` (#523).

### Fixes
1. **A scrape target serving a malformed native histogram over protobuf could crash Prom++.** `ProtobufParser.Histogram()` calls `Compact(0)` before anything validates the payload, and `compactBuckets` assumed the span lengths add up to the bucket count — a histogram with buckets behind only zero-length spans walked past the end of the span slice and panicked (found by `FuzzParseProtobuf`). Compaction is now skipped whenever the spans don't cover exactly as many buckets as the histogram has, and the histogram goes on to `Validate()`, which rejects it with `ErrHistogramSpansBucketsMismatch`; nothing is dropped or rewritten silently. ### Features
1. **Head IDs are now generated as UUIDv7.** `catalog.DefaultIDGenerator` returns a UUIDv7 instead of a random UUIDv4, falling back to v4 if generation fails. A UUIDv7 starts with a millisecond timestamp, so head directories and catalog records now sort lexicographically in creation order, which makes reading the data directory and debugging much easier. The format is unchanged (RFC 4122, 36 characters), so existing heads, catalog records and log files need no migration (#519).
2. **Prom++ can now report that it is running with a feature set other than the expected one.** The new optional `PROMPP_FEATURES_DEFAULT` environment variable holds the expected set; at startup it is compared with `PROMPP_FEATURES` and the result is exposed as the `prompp_features_differ_from_default` gauge — `1` when they differ, `0` when they match — registered only when the variable is set. A mismatch is also logged at warn level with `added` / `removed` / `changed` fields, so it is clear what exactly drifted. The comparison ignores order, whitespace and empty tokens and compares values by meaning: `default_sample_age_limit=60m` equals `=1h`, `head_read_concurrency` equals `head_read_concurrency=1` (#523).

1. **A scrape target serving a malformed native histogram over protobuf could crash Prom++.** `ProtobufParser.Histogram()` calls `Compact(0)` before anything validates the payload, and `compactBuckets` assumed the span lengths add up to the bucket count — a histogram with buckets behind only zero-length spans walked past the end of the span slice and panicked (found by `FuzzParseProtobuf`). Compaction is now skipped whenever the spans don't cover exactly as many buckets as the histogram has, and the histogram goes on to `Validate()`, which rejects it with `ErrHistogramSpansBucketsMismatch`; nothing is dropped or rewritten silently. Upstream Prometheus guards only the case where every span is zero-length (#520).
2. **A `head.log` migration would have wiped the catalog.** `createSwapFile` opened the swap file `O_WRONLY`, but after a migration or a compaction that file becomes the working `FileLog` and has to be readable too: `catalog.sync` read right after `NewFileLog`, got `bad file descriptor`, concluded the log was corrupted and overwrote `head.log` with an empty one — losing the active head, the rotated heads not yet persisted and the remote write positions. It never fired in production, because the log is opened as V2 and no migration takes place, but it blocked moving `head.log` to V3 (#518).
3. **`moment` updated to 2.31.0 in the web UI**, closing GHSA-4p3w-j4w9-5jqw — a path traversal through a crafted non-string locale name.

### Performance
1. **A rotated head no longer carries its ingestion lookup structures until retention.** They are released in two stages, each at the earliest safe point. On rotation, once the old head is read-only, the label set → ls id hash set and the relabeler input LSS are freed: only relabeling on the active head and the shrink during the added-series copy need them, and both are finished by then. After a successful persist, the sorted ls id set is freed as well — it has to survive until the block is written, because `ChunkRecoder` and `RevertableLoader` iterate it, and it is kept for the retry if the persist or the status update fails. Rotated heads loaded from disk on restart skip the rotator but still free both. These structures cost several bytes per series per LSS and used to stay allocated while the new active head was already growing, so this lowers both the peak right after rotation and the steady-state memory of every rotated head (#522, #527).
2. **Rotation no longer makes the first commit of the new head expensive.** The first WAL segment of a new head holds the label sets of every series copied from the old head, so finalizing it costs far more than a regular commit — and it used to happen on the first `Commit` of the already active head, through fastcgo (which occupies the P for the whole call, blocking the Go scheduler and delaying GC stop-the-world) while holding the WAL encoder lock and the LSS read lock, i.e. blocking both the ingest path and new series. That segment is now committed, flushed and synced for every shard right after the added series are copied, before the new head goes live, through a regular cgo call that releases the P. Shards run concurrently, up to `GOMAXPROCS` at a time; a failure is logged and rotation continues. Rotation itself takes longer as a result, while the old head keeps accepting writes. The new `prompp_rotator_head_wal_encoder_long_finalize_duration_nanoseconds` metric reports the longest such call (#525).
3. **Encoding became about 10% faster.** The combined Gorilla path is gone from `DataStorage` — every encoder now keeps timestamps and values in separate streams. The Gorilla codec itself stays and is still used elsewhere. The `prompp_data_storage_gorilla_count` metric is removed along with the path (#515).

## 0.160.0

### 🛑 Breaking changes 🛑

- `operator, collector, target allocator`: Disable operator, collector, and target allocator network policies by default. (#5551, #5558, #5621, #5624, #5654)
  The `operator.networkpolicy` and `operand.networkpolicy` feature gates are moved back to alpha and are disabled by default.
  The generated network policies can block API server access on some clusters.
  To keep creating network policies, enable them with `--feature-gates=+operator.networkpolicy,+operand.networkpolicy`,
  or set `spec.networkPolicy.enabled: true` on individual collectors and target allocators.
  

### 🚩 Deprecations 🚩

- `auto-instrumentation`: Remove autoinstrumentation-php image definition from the repository (#932)
  The PHP autoinstrumentation image will be hosted by the packaging SIG.
  The one released image (v0.1.0) of the image in the operator registry will
  eventually be deleted. This image was never used for any functionality shipped by the operator.

### 💡 Enhancements 💡

- `collector`: Add RBAC support for extracting labels and annotations from CronJobs (and Jobs) via the `k8sattributes` processor. (#5527)
  The operator's own ServiceAccount must itself hold `get`/`list`/`watch` on `batch/jobs` and
  `batch/cronjobs` for this to take effect, since Kubernetes RBAC only lets a ServiceAccount
  grant permissions it already has. This PR also extends the operator's own ClusterRole
  accordingly (`config/rbac/role.yaml`).
  
- `collector, target allocator`: Add `enableServiceLinks` to the OpenTelemetryCollector and TargetAllocator CRs, passed through to the pod spec of the generated workloads. It defaults to true, matching the Kubernetes Pod field. (#5569)
- `operator`: Add support for Kubernetes 1.37 (#5650)

### 🧰 Bug fixes 🧰

- `auto-instrumentation`: Honor Instrumentation CRD/API json tags when loading `--config-file` (no-CRD webhook configs). (#5618)
  Operator Config fields still load with gopkg.in/yaml.v3 (yaml tags). The
  `instrumentations` block is re-parsed with sigs.k8s.io/yaml so embedded API
  types keep their json tags (for example `apacheHttpd`, `imagePullPolicy`,
  `resourceAttributes`, `valueFrom`, `volumeLimitSize`, `configPath`).
  
- `collector`: Preserve TCP and UDP protocols when generating NetworkPolicy ports. (#5611)
- `target allocator`: Use the `.svc` FQDN for the TargetAllocator endpoint injected into the collector's Prometheus receiver so it works on clusters behind an HTTP proxy. (#5586)
  The bare service name (http://<name>-targetallocator:80) does not match the standard NO_PROXY
  entries (.svc, .cluster.local), so Go routes the request through the proxy. Using
  <name>-targetallocator.<namespace>.svc matches NO_PROXY=.svc while staying compatible with
  custom cluster domains (unlike the full .svc.cluster.local endpoint reverted in #3248).
  
- `target allocator`: Restore `promhttp_metric_handler_requests_total` and `promhttp_metric_handler_requests_i
